items.title: Parents take children out of big schools
items.text: More Danish parents are pulling their children out of mainstream schools. They argue that the traditional education system is far too rigid for neurodivergent kids. Children with autism or attention disorders, like 12-year-old Olav, often struggle with noisy classrooms and fixed daily schedules. Because public schools lack resources and specialized programs, many families have turned to alternative support systems, such as parent-led clubs. These spaces allow children to learn at their own pace through practical activities, like organic farming, while giving them a safe environment free from pressure. While politicians worry about falling academic standards in reading and math, educational researchers argue that the school system itself needs urgent reform rather than forcing children to fit into outdated models. These alternative clubs aim to rebuild confidence and help kids rebuild their relationship with learning. Difficult words: rigid (unable to be changed or adapted; strictly set), neurodivergent (having a brain that processes information differently than what is considered typical), academic standards (the levels of quality, knowledge, and achievement expected from students in school). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

items.title: Parents take children out of big schools
items.text: In Denmark, more and more parents are keeping their children home from traditional schools. Many neurodivergent children, like 12-year-old Olav, who has autism, find normal classrooms too loud and stressful. Because schools lack special resources, parents are creating alternative clubs. In these clubs, kids can learn outside by doing practical things, like working on organic farms or building boats, without feeling stressed. While government officials worry about test scores in reading and math, experts say the school system is old and needs big changes. Parents hope these new groups will give their kids a safe space to grow, feel happy again, and slowly return to learning. Difficult words: neurodivergent (thinking, learning, or behaving differently from most other people), lack (to not have enough of something, or to be completely without it), test score (a number or mark that shows how well a student did on an exam). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Parents take children out of big schools
items.text: Many parents in Denmark are taking their kids out of big schools. Normal classrooms are too loud and hard for some children. A boy named Olav has autism . He only goes to school a few hours a week. He mostly learns outside on a farm with his family. Parents are starting local groups where kids can play, work with their hands, and feel safe without stress. Experts say that schools need to change because kids learn in different ways today. These groups help families stay happy and keep learning every day. Difficult words: loud (not quiet), autism (a change in a person’s brain which impacts thinking, speaking, and understanding the world), local (when something is in an area or neighborhood near you). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Hackers attack Ukrainian and Russian emergency apps
items.text: Both Ukraine and Russia recently reported that their official emergency alert apps were hit by major cyberattacks, which triggered mass panic through fake notifications. In Kyiv, citizens received terrifying false warnings about nuclear radiation, chemical threats, and active street fighting, and they were told to stay inside. Ukrainian officials quickly blamed Russian hackers and reassured the public that the actual air defense systems were never compromised . Just hours later, Russia’s Ministry of Emergency Situations reported a similar cyberattack on its own app, which sent out fake alerts with Ukrainian phrasing and offensive language. These attacks target popular mobile apps that millions rely on daily as a backup to air raid sirens . Experts point out that both countries have advanced hacking teams, and digital sabotage is a key weapon for wearing down morale , creating chaos, and making ordinary people doubt official safety warnings on both sides of the war. Difficult words: compromised (weakened, damaged, or made vulnerable to unauthorized access or security failure), air raid siren (a loud device used to warn the public of an incoming air attack or missile threat), sabotage (destroying or damaging something on purpose to stop it from working), morale (the confidence, enthusiasm, and discipline of a person or group at a particular time). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

items.title: Hackers attack Ukrainian and Russian emergency apps
items.text: Both Ukraine and Russia say hackers attacked their official emergency apps with fake safety warnings. People in Ukraine got scary messages on their phones about radiation , chemical danger, and street fights. Officials told everyone it was a fake message from Russian hackers and said their air defense was completely safe. A few hours later, Russia said its own emergency app was also hacked, and people got messages in Ukrainian. Millions of people use these mobile apps every day to stay safe from real attacks. Experts say these digital attacks are meant to scare people, create confusion , and make people lose trust in official warning systems on both sides of the war. Difficult words: radiation (dangerous energy from a nuclear bomb or other objects), air defense (rockets and systems which shoot down planes, rockets, or drones), confusion (a situation in which people are uncertain or don’t understand what is happening). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Hackers attack Ukrainian and Russian emergency apps
items.text: Hackers attack emergency phone apps in Ukraine and Russia. People get scary fake messages on their phones about a nuclear attack , bad air, and street fights. Officials in Kyiv tell people not to worry. They say that the messages are fake. A short time later, people in Russia also get strange fake messages. Millions of people use these apps every day to stay safe. Experts say that hackers do this to scare people, make life hard, and stop people from trusting official safety news. It is a new way for both sides to fight online. Difficult words: nuclear attack (an attack by a nuclear rocket), strange (unusual, hard to understand), scare (to make someone worry or be afraid). items.title: Man completes 28-year walk around the world
items.text: A British man has completed an amazing 28-year walk around the world. Former soldier Karl Bushby, 57, arrived home in the city of Hull in England on Monday. He started his adventure in November 1998 in Chile, South America. His plan was to walk all the way home without using cars, boats, buses, trains, or airplanes. During his journey, he travelled about 58,000 kilometres through 29 countries. He crossed frozen seas, deserts, mountains, and jungles. He also faced many dangers. These included encountering polar bears and kidnappers, and spending time in a Russian prison. His journey was expected to take 12 years. However, problems with money, visas, and borders made his trip a lot longer. Thousands of people welcomed Mr Bushby home. He was very happy to finally finish his journey. His mother was waiting outside his childhood home to greet him. Bushby joked: "Sorry to keep you waiting." He also told the cheering crowd that many people around the world had helped him get home. He said he could not have done it alone. Britain's Prime Minister congratulated him on his achievement. He praised Bushby's determination and belief in himself. Bushby told the Guardian newspaper that he wasn't so interested in walking. He said: "It's boring as hell." That didn't stop him walking across four continents. items.title: Study finds majority of pilots nod off mid-flight
items.text: A new report has raised serious concerns about pilot fatigue. The European Cockpit Association (ECA) conducted a survey of nearly 7,200 pilots across 32 countries. It discovered that exhaustion in the cockpit is a widespread and underreported problem. More than three-quarters of respondents said they had briefly dozed off while operating an aircraft in the month before the survey. Almost a quarter of them admitted they continued flying even when they were too tired. Furthermore, half said they had operated a flight when they should have declared themselves unfit for duty. Tiredness can result from long working hours, insufficient rest, and unpredictable schedules. The pilots were very frank in their answers to the survey questions. Many said they were reluctant to report fatigue because they feared punishment or other negative reactions from their bosses. Captain Coen George, a director of the ECA, warned: "When pilots fear career consequences, fatigue goes unreported and the risk returns to the cockpit." Aviation safety experts say exhaustion can impair judgement, slow reaction times and prevent pilots from responding effectively to unexpected in-flight situations. The experts urged airlines to foster a culture in which pilots can report tiredness without fear of repercussions. Carriers should ensure that passenger safety is their top priority. items.title: World-famous London shopping street pedestrianized
items.text: One of London's most famous shopping streets has been pedestrianized. This means no cars, buses, trucks, or motorbikes can enter it. The street is called Oxford Street. It is well known all over the world. It used to be full of traffic. The Mayor of London, Sir Sadiq Khan, decided to make it pedestrian-only. Around one kilometre of the street is off limits to vehicles. However, delivery trucks can use the area between midnight and 7 am. Mayor Khan hopes the pedestrianization will bring more shoppers back to the area. He called it a very important event for London. Mr Khan also plans to plant more trees along the street, create public squares, and add more seats and tables. There have been mixed reactions to the pedestrianization of Oxford Street. Many people support the plan. They are happy that the area will be less polluted. Khan said a traffic-free Oxford Street would "unlock the full potential" of an important area of London and help make a better, greener, and richer London. Around half a million people visit the street every day. However, many Londoners are unhappy that the street has been closed to traffic. Local official Tim Barnes said: "Traffic will be pushed to the small streets nearby causing economic and environmental harm." The Spectator magazine warned that life for car drivers would be harder. items.title: Mummy removed from exhibition over 'lack of consent'
items.text: A museum in Scotland has removed the remains of an ancient Egyptian mummy from an exhibition because there is no documented evidence that the deceased gave consent for their remains to be displayed. Glasgow's Kelvingrove Art Gallery and Museum took away the remains of a priest named Nakht, a mummified male head, and other body parts. In place of the exhibits, visitors found signs explaining that the remains had been removed "as a mark of respect". The museum said the decision "reflects contemporary museum practice". It added: "In the absence of consent, we believe removing ancient Egyptian human remains from display is more respectful to the deceased individuals." The decision has provoked widespread criticism. Scottish politician Murdo Fraser called the move "woke madness". He argued that museums should showcase history rather than hide it. A museum visitor complained that his daughter was upset at not being able to see the exhibits. An education campaigner said the decision "represents the triumph of educational stupidity and ignorance". He added: "It is not possible to seek permission from those who died thousands of years ago." However, the museum defended its action. It cited the International Council of Museums' Code of Ethics, which says museums "should uphold the inherent dignity of human remains". Buy my 1,000 Ideas and Activities for Language Teachers eBook. items.title: Patrick Stewart dies
items.text: Tributes have poured in from around the world following the death of renowned British actor Sir Patrick Stewart at the age of 86. His close friend and co-star Sir Ian McKellen praised him as one of the most respected actors of his generation. Stewart built a legendary career that seamlessly bridged classical Shakespearean theater and massive Hollywood blockbusters. Although he earned international fame playing Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek and Professor Charles Xavier in X-Men , he always remained deeply connected to his stage roots at the Royal Shakespeare Company. Directors and fellow actors remembered him as a generous collaborator who brought immense humanity, discipline, and accessibility to every role he played, and his passing marks a huge loss for stage and screen. His final film performance will serve as a lasting farewell to fans worldwide. Difficult words: seamlessly (smoothly and continuously), collaborator (a person who works jointly with others on a project or activity), farewell (saying goodbye). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

items.title: Patrick Stewart dies
items.text: Famous British actor Sir Patrick Stewart passed away at the age of 86. Many friends and fans are sharing kind words about his life and work. Actor Ian McKellen called him a deeply loved and respected friend. Stewart became famous around the world for his main roles in Star Trek and the X-Men movies, but he also loved playing in classical theater and performed in many famous Shakespeare plays in Britain. People who worked with him say he was a very talented, kind, and hardworking actor who made deep stories easy for everyone to enjoy. Fans will always remember his great voice, his classic movies, and his famous theater roles. Difficult words: classical theater (traditional plays and dramatic art), perform (to act, sing, dance, or play music in front of people). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Patrick Stewart dies
items.text: Famous actor Sir Patrick Stewart dies at age 86. Many people around the world are sad today. Stewart is famous for his big roles in Star Trek and X-Men movies. He also loves acting on stage in big theater shows. His close friends say that he is a kind man. He loves his work very much. People love listening to his deep voice and watching him act. He shows that you can do big action movies and also play in old story plays on stage. Fans will miss him, but they can still watch his great films. Difficult words: sad (unhappy), stage (an area in a theater where actors are), miss (to feel sad because someone or something is no longer somewhere). items.title: A bull in a car
items.text: In Norfolk, the United States, police were surprised when they received reports of a man driving with a cow in his car, only to discover a massive Watusi bull as the passenger. This breed of African cattle is known for its gigantic horns. The driver, Lee Meyer, was stopped by the police, who issued him a warning due to the unusual and potentially unsafe situation. The bull named Howdy Doody could only fit in the car after modifications were made, including removing parts of the car’s body and windshield and installing a platform. The incident drew attention from onlookers, and it’s unclear where the bull and the driver were heading. Difficult words: breed (a particular type of animal or plant), modification (change), windshield (a window at the front of a car). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

items.title: A bull in a car
items.text: In Norfolk, the United States, the police responded to reports of a man driving with a cow in his car. When they stopped the car, they were surprised to find a massive Watusi bull as the passenger. The police issued the driver a warning due to the unusual situation, which could possibly cause an accident. The bull’s name was Howdy Doody, and the driver had to make some changes in his car to fit the bull in. This incident attracted attention from onlookers who called the police. It’s unclear where the bull and the driver were going. Difficult words: massive (very big), attention (when people are interested in something), onlooker (a person who sees something happen). items.title: New EU deforestation law
items.text: The EU’s anti-deforestation law faces an enforcement test ahead of its launch on 30 December 2026. Under the new rules, companies selling goods such as palm oil, coffee, and cocoa must prove their products are not linked to land cleared after 2020. However, recent investigations by Indonesian environmental organizations reveal that major international consumer brands risk breaching these regulations. Reports show that companies like PepsiCo, Unilever, and Ferrero have bought palm oil from Indonesian plantations accused of recent illegal deforestation. Despite heavy political pressure and lobbying from major exporting nations like the United States and Indonesia to delay or soften the legislation, environmental activists insist the EU must strictly enforce the rules. Indonesia has lost vast areas of forest to illegal logging and agricultural clearing, which increased its vulnerability to severe wildfires. Experts emphasize that strict enforcement by European authorities will be essential to hold global corporations accountable and halt worldwide forest destruction. Difficult words: enforcement (compelling compliance with a law), lobby (to influence a politician or public official on an issue), vulnerability (the possibility of being attacked, damaged, or harmed). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

items.title: New EU deforestation law
items.text: The EU will start using new anti-deforestation rules on 30 December 2026. Companies which sell products like palm oil, coffee, and chocolate must prove they don’t cut down trees to make them. But environmental groups in Indonesia found that big international brands may be breaking these rules. Well-known companies like PepsiCo and Unilever recently bought palm oil from plantations linked to illegal forest clearing. Some countries, including the US and Indonesia, asked the EU to make the rules easier for businesses. But environmental activists say Europe must stay strong and enforce the law. Indonesia lost many forests to farming and fires, so strict checks are needed to protect nature and stop global forest destruction. Difficult words: anti-deforestation (about preventing or stopping the clearing of forests), brand (a product made by a company under a particular name), enforce (to make sure that a rule is followed).
